name: Zimbabwe
summary_text: Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The offence covers sodomy and, per the Human Dignity Trust country profile, acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so conduct short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.  Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries', examines rising anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it covers, Zimbabwe among them. The report's finding of law being deployed as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context for a visitor, alongside the statutory exposure itself.  Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 the Zimbabwean health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, recording that nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor this means formal policy guarantees health-service access, including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.  GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990 with more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, provides legal support explicitly covering arrests for 'sodomy', counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling remain reachable for an LGBTI traveller despite criminalisation.
